transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-08-07
- Time: 16:00 PDT
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Sophie Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Hannah Lee (Redwood), Jared Kim (Citrine CTO), Aisha Rahman (Lead ML), Tom Hu (Platform), Leah Ortiz (Product)

Summary:
Quick developer handoff / hosted chat basics walkthrough focusing on streaming behavior, generation params, and retry/backoff patterns. Customer is evaluating a pilot for in-app conversational search and triage; primary concerns are 1) sub-200ms token latency for short responses, 2) predictable cost under bursty traffic, and 3) network/VPC constraints for Private/Dedicated.

Topics covered:
- Hosted API quickstart and SDK snippets
- Streaming vs sync responses and client-side handling
- Parameters: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, stop sequences, and system prompts
- Retry strategies, idempotency, and backoff with tokens counting
- Console view: per-route cost, token breakdown, traces
- Basic benchmark script and pilot next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sophie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Sophie, AE on the account, Marco is our SE who will walk through the hosted API behavior and streaming examples.
[00:18] Jared (Citrine): Thanks. We wanted this to be practical — engineering handoff so we can run a few smoke benchmarks and then decide between hosted vs a dedicated reserved pool.
[00:30] Marco (Redwood SE): Great, thanks Jared. I'll start with a short demo of a streaming chat request from the hosted API, then we can go into params and retry patterns. If anything sounds too high level tell me to slow down.
[00:45] Marco: Alright, natively you can do a streaming websocket or server-sent events; our SDK also provides a stream iterator. I'll paste a curl streaming example in the shared notes — basically you open the stream, you get deltas for tokens. Important for clients: treat partial deltas as append-only and only commit when stream ends or when you're comfortable with partials.
[01:12] Aisha (Customer): Quick question — do partial tokens count toward billing?
[01:18] Marco: Billing is per token emitted; partials that end up being emitted are counted. If you cancel a response mid-stream the emitted tokens still show up in cost. We have token-level breakdown in the Console per request so you can correlate cost.
[01:38] Tom (Customer): Our latency goal is around 150-200ms for short replies — is that realistic on hosted?
[01:45] Marco: For short responses (single-shot, few tokens) hosted can hit sub-200ms on optimized models in many regions; that depends on model choice and seq length. In practice we recommend measuring p95 over your payload distribution. We also show latency histograms in the Console which help.
[02:03] Leah (Product): What's the tradeoff if we pick a smaller/cheaper model? We want cost predictability.
[02:10] Marco: Lower-capacity models reduce cost but increase latency and may degrade quality. For deterministic short replies you can use quantized model variants — Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and batching settings based on your workload.
[02:25] Sophie: I'll flag that Optimize integration so you can see recommendations after the pilot.
[02:31] Marco: Now params — simple ones: max_tokens, temperature, top_p, presence_penalty. For short assistant replies keep temperature around 0.0–0.3 and max_tokens small. Also make use of stop sequences to early-terminate generation — that helps cost.
[02:52] Aisha: Do you recommend system messages vs adding context in the first user message?
[02:56] Marco: System messages are better for global instructions; client-side context for immediate user state. For streaming and smaller token budgets, keep system prompts minimal.
[03:12] Marco: I'm going to demo a streaming session — note the SDK's resume/ids feature. We provide a request id header you can persist.
[03:25] [screen share noise] Marco: (typing) Here's a live curl stream example... you'll see chunked deltas come every ~10-30ms while decoding.
[03:40] Jared: I'm seeing in our tests intermittent 5xx errors when we hit bursts, what should we do?
[03:46] Marco: Good question. Best practice is exponential backoff with jitter and idempotency keys where applicable. For generation endpoints you can re-try idempotently for short-lived requests with the same input, but be aware of duplicate tokens if retries are not deduped server-side. We recommend the client use a unique request ID and the server checks for duplicate request ids for safe retries where business logic allows.
[04:12] Tom: How do you recommend handling partial replies and reconnections?
[04:17] Marco: Two patterns — 1) client buffers partial tokens and on reconnect attempts to fetch the remaining tail using the conversation state (we allow resume tokens in some setups), 2) client restarts a short generation and heuristically dedups. We log at the trace level to help debug replays.
[04:40] Aisha: Any limits on concurrent streams per API key?
[04:44] Sophie: There are rate limits which depend on plan; hosted free tiers are lower, enterprise can increase concurrency. We'll share the rate limit table in the docs link.
[04:55] Marco: Switching to retry semantics — statu codes: 429 is throttling, 5xx is server errors. For 429s backoff then retry; for 5xx try once with backoff, if it persists consider routing to a fallback model (we support automatic fallback config to a cheaper replica).
[05:15] Leah: Is that automatic fallback something we need Dedicated to use?
[05:18] Marco: No, hosted supports fallback policies. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity which reduces throttling risk. Private on-prem gives you complete control.
[05:30] Jared: Our security folks ask about audit logs and KMS — can hosted integrate with our KMS?
[05:35] Sophie: For hosted we support customer-managed keys for encryption-at-rest in enterprise tiers and comprehensive audit logs; Private/Dedicated have stronger network controls. We'll send the SOC2 and audit docs.
[05:50] Tom: For pilot, we'll likely start hosted and if constraints show up we'll evaluate Dedicated.
[05:55] Marco: Sounds sensible. Next I'll show an example of parameter tuning for cost. If you batch short requests you get cost savings but at the expense of tail latency. Redwood's batching engine is workload-aware; the Console Optimize tab suggests batch sizes.
[06:18] Marco: Example: if you have many 10-token requests, batching them reduces kernel overhead. But for synchronous UX you may not want to add 50ms of queueing. That's where the routing policy helps — route low-latency traffic to smaller batches, lower-priority to batch pool.
[06:33] Aisha: How do we configure routing policies?
[06:36] Marco: In the Console under Deployments > Routes. You can set per-route latency SLOs, fallback model lists, and cost thresholds. We'll include a short video clip in the shared folder.
[06:48] [noise/interruption] Sophie: Quick pause — Marco will drop two links in chat: the hosted API quickstart and the benchmark script.
[06:55] Marco: (chat) https://app.redwood.com/docs/hosted-api-quickstart and https://drive.redwood.com/shared/citrine-benchmarks (note: placeholder).
[07:10] Jared: Thanks. Can you quickly show the Console trace view?
[07:14] Marco: Yep. (screenshare) Here's a request trace with token-level timing, host kernel selection, and cache hit/miss info. Notice the KV cache column — sorry that's our internal naming, it's sometimes transcribed as K V cash in older logs.
[07:36] Tom: KV cache miss rate matters, how do we improve that?
[07:40] Marco: Keep shared prefixes short and reuse context. For chat apps, pass conversation history but trim older messages. Redwood's prefix caching will retain popular prefixes in memory; the Console shows prefix hit rates.
[07:55] Aisha: For our evaluation, we'll want a script that runs representative user flows; can you recommend sample durations and concurrency?
[08:02] Marco: Yes — run a 10-minute ramp with steady-state concurrency near your expected peak, plus a 2-minute burst test at 3x to see throttling. We'll provide a shell script that hits the convo endpoint and records p50/p95/p99.
[08:20] Leah: Is there an easy way to compare cost across models in the Console?
[08:24] Marco: Console Optimize has a cost simulation where you upload a few sample prompts and it projects cost across model variants and quantization options. That's part of Redwood Optimize.
[08:35] Jared: Great. Aisha: Any gotchas about tokenization? Our prompts include non-English and emojis.
[08:42] Marco: Tokenization affects token count and cost. Use the tokenizer tool in the SDK to simulate token counts. Emojis and non-Latin scripts can increase tokenization variance. We'll share tokenizer samples.
[08:55] Aisha: About retries again — what about duplicate side-effects? Like creating tickets twice if user replays a request?
[09:01] Marco: For side-effects you should implement idempotency at the application layer. Use unique action ids in your business payload and make the server check for duplicates. For long-running side-effects consider asynchronous job models and use the LLM only for generation, not execution.
[09:18] Tom: Do you have an example SDK pattern for client-side dedup?
[09:22] Marco: Yes, we'll include a small snippet showing generating a uuid per user action and attaching it as metadata.
[09:28] [10:00 mark - montage of questions and answers condensed]
[10:00] Marco: Quick note on streaming backpressure: when a client can't keep up, we recommend enabling small buffer windows and applying application-level flow-control; the SDK emits buffer-full events.
[11:12] Sophie: Quick commercial note — pilot pricing typically covers X tokens per month and a short-term evaluation credit; I'll send details.
[12:01] Jared: If we see quality regressions during pilot, can we roll back model versions easily?
[12:07] Marco: Yes, sandbox and production routes can pin model versions and we do canary rollouts. The Console supports manual or automated rollback on quality regression triggers.
[12:24] Leah: How do you surface quality regressions?
[12:27] Marco: Redwood Optimize lets you tie evals to prompt sets and will alert on BLEU/ROUGE or custom metrics regressions. You can also set automated traffic splitting between versions.
[12:40] Aisha: Will Optimize suggest quantization aggressively? We're nervous about hallucinations.
[12:46] Marco: Optimize balances cost vs quality. For hallucination-sensitive tasks we recommend conservative quantization and running evals on critical prompts. We'll provide quantization profiles per model.
[13:05] Tom: Network planning — if we decide on Dedicated, how does peering work?
[13:10] Marco: Dedicated supports VPC peering and private link. For Private on-prem we can provide an installer and air-gapped options.
[13:20] Leah: For pilot, what data residency options are available?
[13:24] Sophie: Hosted regions include NA and EU regions; Dedicated and Private give you more control. We'll capture your residency needs in the SOW.
[13:34] Jared: Ok can you summarize the suggested pilot next steps?
[13:37] Sophie: Sure — run a 2-week hosted pilot with sample prompts, shared benchmark script, and Console access for telemetry. We'll review results and recommend Dedicated or Private if needed.
[13:48] Marco: I'll drop the benchmark script and a checklist: sample prompt set, expected SLAs, token budgets, concurrency targets.
[14:00] Aisha: Any final questions from our infra folks?
[14:05] Tom: Proxying — we have an outbound proxy that mutates TLS. Any known issues?
[14:09] Marco: Some proxies that terminate TLS can break streaming. If you have a terminating proxy you'll want to enable TLS passthrough or place a NAT egress to avoid middleboxes altering chunking. We'll send a short note on proxy configs.
[14:25] Leah: That's good. Also please share the Console demo recording.
[14:29] Marco: Will do.
[14:32] [silence — final notes]
[14:40] Sophie: Recap and owners — Sophie will share pricing and SOC2 docs; Marco shares benchmark script and example SDK snippets; Aisha provides prompt sets; Tom shares network constraints. We'll reconvene after pilot results.
[14:55] Jared: Perfect, thanks all.
[15:00] Sophie: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and scheduling.
